nodes.name: Stationary point ambiguity
nodes.description: A stationary point can be a global minimizer, a poor local minimizer, or a saddle point; first-order information alone does not distinguish among these possibilities.

nodes.name: Near-zero gradient regions far from global solutions
nodes.description: In highly non-convex landscapes, large regions of near-zero gradient may exist far from any global solution.

nodes.name: Gradient-based methods can stagnate misleadingly
nodes.description: Algorithms following gradient-based dynamics can stagnate in near-zero-gradient regions, producing iterates certified as theoretically successful while being arbitrarily suboptimal in objective value.

nodes.name: Stationarity is a weak proxy for optimization progress
nodes.description: Because stationary points can be far from global solutions and gradient-based methods can get stuck there, stationarity-based guarantees are a weak proxy for actual optimization success.

nodes.name: Empirical gradient norm stagnation observed
nodes.description: In long training runs of modern ML models, the gradient norm has been observed not to decrease, and in some cases to increase, toward the end of training.

nodes.name: Central motivating question
nodes.description: This state of affairs motivates the central question of the paper: how to obtain global convergence guarantees for non-convex problems without relying on gradient-based dynamics and gradient-norm metrics.

nodes.name: Perturbation/noise methods remain fundamentally local
nodes.description: Escaping stationary points via explicit perturbed-gradient methods or implicit mini-batch noise typically yields guarantees that remain fundamentally local, at best ensuring convergence to approximate second-order stationary points.

nodes.name: BPM as trust-region-style ball oracle method
nodes.description: The Ball Proximal Point Method (BPM) is a trust-region-type method where each iterate is obtained by minimizing the objective over a ball of radius t centered at the current point, via the set-valued broximal operator.

nodes.name: BPM converges linearly without strong convexity
nodes.description: BPM was found to converge linearly without the strong convexity assumptions required by methods like the classical Proximal Point Method (PPM).

nodes.name: BPM can attain exact global minimum in finite steps
nodes.description: Unlike PPM with finite steps, which can only produce approximate solutions, BPM can attain the exact global minimum in a finite number of iterations using finite radii.

nodes.name: Existing BPM analyses focus on convex objectives
nodes.description: Despite BPM's strong convergence guarantees and evidence that it can handle non-convexity, existing analyses focus almost exclusively on convex objectives, with only limited non-convex treatment.

nodes.name: Paper revisits BPM to study non-convex global convergence
nodes.description: Motivated by the gap between BPM's demonstrated non-convex potential and its convex-focused existing analysis, this paper revisits BPM to identify structural conditions enabling global convergence in the non-convex setting.

nodes.name: Broximal oracle is generally intractable
nodes.description: The broximal oracle is very powerful and generally intractable: if the radius is sufficiently large, a global solution can be found in one step, meaning solving the subproblem can be as hard as solving the original problem.

nodes.name: BPM treated as conceptual tool, not practical algorithm
nodes.description: Because the broximal oracle is generally intractable, the paper treats BPM as a conceptual tool for isolating a novel class of non-convex functions for which global convergence can be established, rather than as a practical algorithm.

nodes.name: Second Brox Theorem exploits convexity
nodes.description: The original convex analysis of BPM relies on the Second Brox Theorem, which shows that for convex f there exists a coefficient such that a specific inner-product inequality holds between the current point, the broximal update, and any reference point.

nodes.name: Specializing to global minimizer yields nonnegative inner product
nodes.description: Specializing the Second Brox Theorem's inequality to the reference point being a global minimizer yields a nonnegative inner-product relation between the step direction and the direction to that minimizer.

nodes.name: Observation motivates dropping convexity, positing inequality directly
nodes.description: This observation motivates dropping convexity altogether and instead directly postulating the geometric alignment inequality as an assumption (Assumption 3.1), independent of any convexity assumption.

nodes.name: Assumption 3.1: geometric alignment condition
nodes.description: Assumption 3.1 posits that outside a t-neighborhood of the global minimizer set, the inner product between the step direction (x minus broximal update u) and the direction toward a fixed global minimizer is non-positive, i.e., the broximal step is aligned toward the global minimizer.

nodes.name: Relaxation dist(x,Xf) > t is essential for non-uniqueness
nodes.description: The relaxation restricting Assumption 3.1 to points outside the t-neighborhood of the minimizer set is essential; imposing the condition for all x would force uniqueness of the global minimizer.

nodes.name: Assumption 3.1 alone does not rule out broxtf(x)={x} away from Xf
nodes.description: Under Assumption 3.1 alone, having broxtf(x) equal to the singleton {x} does not necessarily imply that x is a global minimizer, leaving a gap that must be addressed by an additional assumption.

nodes.name: Assumption 3.2: no isolated local minima
nodes.description: Assumption 3.2 states that if the broximal operator at x is the singleton {x} (x is a strict minimizer within its own ball), then x must already be a global minimizer, ruling out 'bad' local minima detectable at scale t.

nodes.name: Definition of Broximal Aligned Functions
nodes.description: A proper, closed function belongs to the class of Broximal Aligned Functions if it satisfies both Assumption 3.1 and Assumption 3.2 for a given radius t and geometry X.

nodes.name: Non-decreasing step must be followed by strict decrease
nodes.description: Under Assumption 3.1, as long as the algorithm makes progress (x_k not equal x_{k+1}), a non-decreasing function-value step must be followed by a strict decrease at the next step.

nodes.name: Consequent separation distance bound (Lemma A.4)
nodes.description: The non-decrease-then-strict-decrease pattern implies that the distance between iterates two steps apart exceeds the radius t, formalized in Lemma A.4.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.1: every second iterate separated by distance >= t
nodes.description: Building on Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2, the main convergence theorem (4.1) relies on the fact that every second BPM iterate is separated by a distance of at least t, unless a global minimizer has already been reached.

nodes.name: Distances to minimizer are non-increasing
nodes.description: Theorem 4.1 shows the distances from the iterates to the global minimizer are non-increasing, with a quantified decrease of at least t^2/3 every third iterate when the current ball does not yet contain a global minimizer.

nodes.name: Finite-iteration exact global convergence
nodes.description: Theorem 4.1 concludes that after a sufficient finite number of iterations K (of order the squared initial distance over t^2), the BPM iterate is exactly a global minimizer.

nodes.name: Example 1: |x|+10sin(x) has infinitely many local minima
nodes.description: The one-dimensional function f(x) = |x| + 10*sin(x) has infinitely many local minima spaced every 2*pi, yet satisfies Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 for any radius t >= 2*pi.

nodes.name: Example 1 shows multiple local minima permitted
nodes.description: Example 1 demonstrates that the Broximal Aligned function class does not preclude the existence of multiple local minima, in contrast to classical conditions where all stationary points are globally optimal.

nodes.name: Example 2: disconnected minimizer set
nodes.description: A function with minimizer set Xf = {0, a} for a nonzero vector a is shown to belong to the Broximal Aligned class for any t > 0, despite having a disconnected minimizer set.

nodes.name: Examples 1 and 2 fail all classical conditions
nodes.description: Both Example 1 and Example 2 belong to the Broximal Aligned class for suitable t, yet fail to satisfy any of the classical generalized-convexity conditions listed in the paper's comparison table.

nodes.name: Theorem 5.1: strict quasiconvexity implies Broximal Alignment
nodes.description: Strictly quasiconvex functions belong to the Broximal Aligned class for any radius t > 0.

nodes.name: Theorem 5.2: pseudoconvexity implies Broximal Alignment
nodes.description: Pseudoconvex functions belong to the Broximal Aligned class for any radius t > 0.

nodes.name: Theorem 5.3: quasar convexity implies Broximal Alignment
nodes.description: Functions that are zeta-quasar convex with respect to a global minimizer belong to the Broximal Aligned class for any radius t > 0.

nodes.name: Theorem 5.4: aiming condition with unique minimizer implies Broximal Alignment
nodes.description: Functions satisfying the aiming condition with a unique global minimizer belong to the Broximal Aligned class for any radius t > 0.

nodes.name: Broximal Aligned class strictly subsumes classical non-convex frameworks
nodes.description: Because quasiconvexity, pseudoconvexity, quasar convexity, and aiming (with unique minimizer) all imply Broximal Alignment, while Examples 1 and 2 show functions in the Broximal Aligned class satisfying none of these conditions, the Broximal Aligned framework strictly generalizes these classical non-convex function classes.

nodes.name: Broximal oracle intractable for practical objectives
nodes.description: For many objectives of practical interest, particularly in modern ML, exactly minimizing f over balls B_X(x,t) is computationally intractable.

nodes.name: Approximate broximal subproblem solving
nodes.description: One practical approximation strategy is to approximately solve the broximal subproblem itself, e.g., via sampling-based approaches or an iterative method run up to prescribed accuracy.

nodes.name: Local model substitution (e.g., linearization)
nodes.description: A second practical approximation strategy replaces the original objective with a simpler local model, such as a linearized or quadratic trust-region subproblem, which is often tractable and sometimes has closed-form solutions.

nodes.name: Muon optimizer as approximate broximal step in non-Euclidean geometry
nodes.description: The Muon optimizer can be interpreted as performing approximate broximal steps by minimizing linearized local models over non-Euclidean balls induced by the spectral norm, illustrating that local-model approximations extend beyond the Euclidean setting.

isolated_nodes.name: Non-convex optimization central to ML
isolated_nodes.description: Matrix factorization, phase retrieval, representation learning, and deep neural networks all lead to objective functions with highly non-convex landscapes.

isolated_nodes.name: Non-convex problems can be NP-hard
isolated_nodes.description: Many non-convex optimization tasks are NP-hard to solve, and a number of them are NP-hard even to approximate.

isolated_nodes.name: Convex optimization has efficient global toolkit
isolated_nodes.description: Unlike non-convex optimization, convex optimization has an established toolkit for efficiently finding global minimizers.

isolated_nodes.name: Intermediate convexity relaxations
isolated_nodes.description: A number of intermediate frameworks (star convexity, quasar convexity, pseudoconvexity, quasiconvexity, invexity, variational coherence, the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition, and the aiming condition) retain meaningful convergence properties for broader problem classes than convexity, each with its own limitations.

isolated_nodes.name: Special-structure tractability examples
isolated_nodes.description: Certain non-convex problems become tractable when the objective has special structure, e.g., one-layer neural networks having no spurious local minima, or SGD finding global minima in sufficiently wide over-parameterized networks.

isolated_nodes.name: Particle-based PDE methods for global non-convex solutions
isolated_nodes.description: Particle-based approaches reformulate non-convex problems as PDE-governed dynamics over measures, now admitting provable global solutions, though typically requiring an exponentially large or infinite number of particles.

isolated_nodes.name: Contribution: novel non-convex function class
isolated_nodes.description: The paper introduces a novel class of non-convex functions, Broximal Aligned Functions, defined by Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2, enabling global optimization guarantees beyond gradient-based reasoning.

isolated_nodes.name: Lemma 5.1: monotone transformation preserves assumptions
isolated_nodes.description: If h satisfies Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 for radius t, then composing h with a strictly increasing scalar function g also satisfies Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 with the same t.

isolated_nodes.name: Lemma 5.2: X-orthogonal affine transformations preserve assumptions
isolated_nodes.description: Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 are invariant under affine changes of coordinates that preserve the geometry induced by X.

isolated_nodes.name: Lemma 5.3: affine transformations of function value preserve assumptions
isolated_nodes.description: Scaling and shifting the function value (af(x)+b for a>0) preserves Assumptions 3.1 and 3.2 with the same radius and minimizer set.

isolated_nodes.name: Framework intentionally conceptual, not efficient algorithm
isolated_nodes.description: The framework is intentionally conceptual since the broximal oracle is generally intractable, so the results do not directly yield efficient algorithms, motivating future work on practical approximations.

structural_reasoning: The graph is highly coherent, mirroring the paper's tightly argued theoretical structure: the motivation chain critiquing stationarity-based theory (C1) directly motivates revisiting BPM and identifying its underexplored non-convex potential (C2); the intractability of the general broximal oracle and the convex-case Second Brox Theorem motivate dropping convexity in favor of a direct geometric postulate (C3); this postulate is formalized into the two core assumptions defining the Broximal Aligned function class (C4); the main convergence theorem is derived through a clear proof chain building on these assumptions (C5); concrete examples demonstrate the class's generality beyond classical conditions (C6); formal theorems establish that classical generalized-convexity conditions are special cases (C7); and practical approximation strategies are discussed as a natural coda (C8). Edge confidence is high throughout given the paper's explicit deductive theorem-proof style and clearly stated motivational transitions between sections. The isolated-node set reflects broader contextual and background material (application domains, related relaxations, closure-property lemmas, and general framing statements) that support but are not part of the core technical dependency chain. No cycles or ambiguous directions were identified.
